preferences: Bottom-line diagnostic: before using payoffs, ask whether the model has a stable ordering over the relevant outcomes. If the same three choices create a cycle, utility numbers will only hide the inconsistency. Preferences are the ordering discipline underneath every later payoff table.
utility: Bottom-line diagnostic: when a paper writes payoff numbers, ask what comparisons those numbers are allowed to support. If only ranking matters, many scales can represent the same choices. If spacing matters, the model has added stronger assumptions that need to be named.
expected_utility: Bottom-line diagnostic: when action happens before uncertainty resolves, force the model to keep every possible state visible. Expected utility is not a prediction that the average state occurs; it is the comparison device that weights each possible consequence before choosing.
strategic_form_games: Bottom-line diagnostic: if a payoff is being discussed without naming every player's action in that cell, the strategic form is being misread. The table's purpose is to make interdependence explicit: each outcome is produced by a full action profile.
extensive_form_games: Bottom-line diagnostic: whenever order, observation, or later choice matters, ask whether a flat table has hidden the real problem. A tree earns its keep by showing who moves when, what they know, and where credibility is tested.
dominance: Bottom-line diagnostic: a dominated action loses by comparison, not by vibe. Before deleting it, verify the inequality across every modeled opponent contingency. If the argument uses what the opponent is likely to do, it is belief-based rather than dominance-based.
iterated_deletion: Bottom-line diagnostic: iterated deletion is a reasoning chain, not one big eraser. Each round must be justified by the smaller game produced by earlier justified deletions. The surviving set means not eliminated by that test, not necessarily predicted.
rationalizability: Bottom-line diagnostic: ask whether an action can be made optimal by some coherent belief. If yes, it may be defensible even outside Nash equilibrium. If no belief can rescue it, the action is not merely surprising; it is strategically unjustified. The audit is belief existence, not final coordination.
best_response: Bottom-line diagnostic: never say best response without completing the phrase best against what. The concept is conditional by design. Change the opponent action, belief, type, or history, and the local optimization problem may change with it. A response curve is therefore a family of answers, not one answer.
nash_equilibrium: Bottom-line diagnostic: test stability one player at a time. Freeze everyone else and search for a profitable switch. If none exists for any player, the profile is Nash. That says unilateral regret is gone, not that the outcome is good.
mixed_strategies: Bottom-line diagnostic: randomization is doing strategic work when predictability would be punished. The usual clue is an indifference equation: probabilities are chosen so the opponent cannot profit by targeting one pure action over another. Always check which player's payoffs are being equalized.
zero_sum_games: Bottom-line diagnostic: add the payoffs in every cell before importing zero-sum reasoning. Exact opposition creates security-value logic. If totals vary, the situation may still be competitive, but it is not the pure conflict that minimax arguments require. This boundary keeps adversarial math from swallowing bargaining, markets, or repeated cooperation. The fixed total is the diagnostic, and it explains why one player's gain exactly measures the other player's loss.
minimax: Bottom-line diagnostic: minimax asks what each plan guarantees against the opponent's strongest attack. Use it when adversarial protection is the point. If the opponent has aligned interests, limited information, or likely mistakes, worst-case reasoning may overstate caution. The method chooses a floor, not an expected outcome.
backward_induction: Bottom-line diagnostic: solve the future choice where a threat or promise would actually be carried out. If the future player would not choose it there, the earlier statement should not shape present behavior unless commitment or reputation changes the payoff.
subgame_perfection: Bottom-line diagnostic: Nash at the start is not enough for dynamic games. Jump into each relevant continuation game and rerun the no-deviation test. Subgame perfection rejects strategies that survive only because their threats are never reached. The practical question is whether the plan remains rational after the history it tries to deter.
one_shot_deviation: Bottom-line diagnostic: the one-shot deviation principle is a theorem-backed shortcut, not a universal habit. Change exactly one current action, hold the continuation fixed, and ask whether that local temptation pays under conditions where local checks are sufficient. If the conditions fail, longer deviations may be hiding.
bargaining: Bottom-line diagnostic: separate whether trade creates surplus from how that surplus is divided. Then inspect outside options, patience, and timing. Bargaining power in the model comes from continuation values, not from verbal toughness or moral deservingness. A better fallback can change the split without changing total surplus. Keep those calculations separate.
finitely_repeated_games: Bottom-line diagnostic: a known final round can erase discipline before the final round arrives. Solve the last period first, then move backward. Repetition helps only when future rewards or punishments still have force at the moment of temptation. If cooperation survives, identify the extra post-game or reputation force. Otherwise the endpoint logic returns.
infinitely_repeated_games: Bottom-line diagnostic: indefinite repetition supports cooperation only through an incentive inequality. Compare today's cheating gain with the discounted value of future punishment or lost cooperation. The phrase long relationship does no work unless monitoring and punishment are credible.
folk_theorem: Bottom-line diagnostic: the folk theorem expands what can be supported; it does not select what will happen. Check feasibility, individual rationality, and punishment credibility, then separately ask what institution or convention chooses one supported outcome.
implicit_cartels: Bottom-line diagnostic: high prices can come from tacit repeated-game discipline, but the model is not legal proof of collusion. Identify cheating gains, monitoring quality, and punishment incentives before saying a cartel-like outcome is self-enforcing. Demand noise and entry can break the punishment story.
imperfect_competition: Bottom-line diagnostic: if a firm is large enough that its choice changes rivals' payoffs or market price, single-firm optimization is too small. The key object becomes a reaction problem: each firm's best move depends on the other's move.
bayesian_games: Bottom-line diagnostic: hidden information must be put into the game, not waved at verbally. Name the types, priors, who observes what, and the strategy rule for each type. Otherwise uncertainty becomes an excuse rather than a model. The strategic object is a rule across possible private facts. Average-player reasoning is too coarse.
types_and_beliefs: Bottom-line diagnostic: type is the hidden payoff-relevant fact; belief is someone else's probability story about that fact. Keep them separate. A model becomes informative when observations or equilibrium restrictions discipline how beliefs move. If beliefs can be chosen freely, the explanation is too loose. Ask what pins them down and which observed action should actually change them.
bayesian_nash_equilibrium: Bottom-line diagnostic: equilibrium under hidden information is a rule checked type by type. Do not test only the average player. Hold the other type-contingent rules fixed and ask whether each type has a profitable expected-payoff deviation. One failing type breaks the whole proposed rule. The strategy is a function.
screening_and_adverse_selection: Bottom-line diagnostic: whenever a price, offer, or contract changes who participates, recompute the pool. The old average may be irrelevant after selection. The concept is active when hidden types sort themselves through the rule. Participation is evidence, not just a count of customers.
auctions: Bottom-line diagnostic: a bid has two effects at once: it changes the chance of winning and the surplus if winning. Read the payment rule before drawing conclusions, because first-price, second-price, and platform formats change incentives. A bid is an action under rules, not a value confession.
revenue_equivalence: Bottom-line diagnostic: revenue equivalence is an assumptions result, not an auction slogan. Check allocation sameness, boundary payoff, symmetry, independent private values, and risk neutrality. When the theorem fails, the failing assumption often identifies the economic force. The theorem is most useful as an assumption audit.
ad_auctions: Bottom-line diagnostic: platform auctions allocate attention, not just objects. Keep bid, quality, click probability, slot assignment, and payment separate. If those pieces collapse into one score, the strategic incentives become impossible to inspect. Platform measurement is part of the mechanism, not background plumbing. Ranking and pricing are distinct, and both shape what advertisers learn to manipulate.
perfect_bayesian_equilibrium: Bottom-line diagnostic: PBE requires strategies and beliefs to fit together. On-path beliefs must update by Bayes rule; continuation actions must be optimal under those beliefs. Off-path freedom should be labeled, because it can drive the result. Inspect inference and sequential choice as one object. Neither half is optional.
signaling: Bottom-line diagnostic: a visible action reveals type only if types have different incentives to take it. Always run the imitation test. If the wrong type wants to copy the signal, separation fails and receiver beliefs should reflect pooling. Visibility alone is not information. Incentive separation creates information.
cheap_talk: Bottom-line diagnostic: costless words become informative only when incentives make different messages credible. Ask what every sender type wants the receiver to believe and do. If all types prefer the same message, the talk pools information. Alignment, not eloquence, carries the signal.
common_knowledge: Bottom-line diagnostic: coordination may require shared awareness, not just shared facts. Ask whether players know, know that others know, and know that this is mutual. Publicness is the strategic object; private knowledge may not coordinate behavior.
